item.title: Moody’s cuts Nvidia outlook to stable, saying Huang’s exit clouds strategy and policy
item.description:
On its own, an outlook change rarely moves equity prices, and Nvidia’s balance sheet remains among the strongest in corporate credit. The bigger signal is for bond and CDS investors: protection costs had already climbed as the leadership crisis unfolded, and Moody’s move confirms that governance risk is now being priced into Nvidia’s credit. For the wider AI trade, it is another headwind in a week already focused on Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut and Fed rate risk. Asian suppliers such as TSMC and the memory makers could be sensitive to any sign that Nvidia’s partners are rethinking their ties to the company.

---

Moody’s isn’t questioning Nvidia’s ability to pay its debts, but it is now waiting to see who leads the company and how the board’s investigation ends before it considers an upgrade.

Summary:

  • Moody’s lowered Nvidia’s outlook to stable from positive and called the CEO resignation credit negative
  • The agency cited uncertainty over business strategy and financial policies, and possible knock-on effects for Nvidia’s AI partnerships
  • Moody’s also pointed to governance and operational vulnerabilities, including those linked to export controls
  • Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and director on November 11, effective immediately, after 33 years at the company
  • CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey Jones has been named the board’s first-ever chair
  • The board opened an independent investigation after reports about Huang’s personal conduct, but said it had no reason to believe secrets or national security had been compromised

Moody’s has lowered its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive, saying the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang is credit negative because it has created uncertainty over the chipmaker’s business strategy and financial policies. The change takes a near-term upgrade off the table rather than signalling any weakness in Nvidia’s balance sheet, but it is a pointed signal that the rating agency sees governance, not demand, as the main question hanging over the AI industry’s dominant chip supplier.

Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member on November 11, effective immediately, ending a 33-year run at the company he co-founded. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board has appointed Harvey Jones as its first-ever chair while it searches for a permanent successor. The departure followed reports about Huang’s personal conduct, including an alleged link to a person said to have ties to Chinese intelligence, which led the board to open an independent investigation. The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised.

Moody’s concern goes beyond the change at the top. The agency said the leadership shake-up could also weigh on Nvidia’s growth strategy, which relies heavily on a vast web of relationships across the AI industry, at a time when the company is working to fix governance and operational weak spots, including those linked to US export controls. That last point matters because export rules have already shaped Nvidia’s access to China, and any perception that its controls or oversight fall short could invite closer scrutiny from Washington.

A positive outlook typically means a rating agency sees a meaningful chance of an upgrade within the next year or two. Moving back to stable suggests Moody’s now wants to see who leads Nvidia, how the board’s review concludes and whether the company’s partnerships hold up before it considers a higher rating.

The timing is awkward for the AI trade. Investors are already uneasy about rising interest rates and the cost of funding data centre expansion, and Nvidia sits at the centre of that spending. The next markers to watch are the outcome of the board’s investigation, the choice of a permanent chief executive and any sign that customers or partners are rethinking their ties to the company. 

The torch has passed to Colette Kress, Nvidia's new CEO. It's a tough gig right now. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ tipped to hike to 1.50% in December, its first three-hike year in 37 years
item.description:
With a December hike now the clear consensus, the bigger surprise for the yen would be a hold. That would likely send USD/JPY back toward the levels that prompted heavy intervention. A hike on its own may do little to lift the yen while the Fed is also tightening, so traders are likely to focus on whether Ueda signals the faster path to 1.75% that the poll now expects. Front-end JGB yields have room to rise further if that guidance comes through. The Nikkei faces a double headwind from higher domestic rates and the shaky AI trade, which leaves exporters relying more heavily on a weak yen for support.

--- Japan’s economy is shrinking and its stock market is sliding, but with inflation above target and the yen near 160, economists expect the BOJ to keep hiking, first in December and again by March.

Summary:

  • 86% of economists in a Reuters poll, 61 of 71, expect the BOJ to raise rates 25bp to 1.50% at its December 17 to 18 meeting
  • That would be the first time in 37 years that the BOJ has hiked three times in one calendar year
  • Nearly 60% see a further rise to 1.75% by end-March, three months earlier than forecast in October, and views on the peak are split between 1.75% and 2% or higher
  • Governor Ueda said rates should keep rising, after core inflation returned above 2% in September despite a July to September GDP contraction
  • The yen is back near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion in intervention, and 83% of economists said the Nikkei’s 7% monthly drop would not derail a hike
  • Next year’s spring wage talks are expected to deliver around 5.00%, close to this year’s 5.01%

The Bank of Japan is expected to raise interest rates at its December 17 to 18 meeting and again by the end of March, according to a Reuters poll published on Wednesday, with policymakers judged to be more worried about inflation and a weak yen than about a stumbling economy. Of 71 economists surveyed between November 11 and 18, 61, or 86%, expect the overnight call rate to rise by 25 basis points to 1.50%, three months after the bank’s last move.

That would mark the BOJ’s third hike of 2026, the first time in 37 years it has tightened three times in a single calendar year. The momentum does not stop there. Nearly 60% of respondents expect another quarter point increase to 1.75% by the end of March, three months sooner than economists forecast in October. Opinion on the end point is split down the middle: among those who answered a separate question, about half see 1.75% as the peak, while an equal share expect rates to reach 2% or higher.

The case for pressing on rests on prices and the currency rather than growth. Japan’s economy unexpectedly shrank in the July to September quarter, its first contraction in a year, yet core consumer inflation rose back above the 2% target in September for the first time in nine months. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the central bank should keep raising rates. One economist in the poll said the BOJ still sees large upside risks to prices while financial conditions remain loose, and expects policy to stay on a tightening track.

The yen is the sharpest pressure point. It is back near 160 per dollar even after authorities spent close to $100 billion of reserves defending it, and the Federal Reserve’s own hiking cycle, with another increase expected in December, keeps the interest rate gap wide. That gap leaves the yen prone to further weakness, and one economist warned that skipping a December move could push it lower still and add to imported inflation.

Equity turbulence is not seen as a deal breaker. The Nikkei 225 has fallen about 7% this month, largely on doubts over whether the pace of global AI investment can last, but 83% of respondents to a separate question said the volatility would not stop a December hike. Another economist said a pause remains possible if the AI-driven selloff keeps rattling markets, while still treating a hike as the baseline.

Wages offer the BOJ another reason for confidence. Economists expect next year’s spring labour talks to deliver pay rises of around 5.00%, just below this year’s 5.01%, which would make a fourth straight year of increases at roughly that pace. Forecasts ranged from 4.25% to 5.50%. Sustained wage gains of that size are the kind of evidence the BOJ has long said it needs to keep normalising policy, and they make a December move look like a continuation of a plan rather than a reaction to the yen alone. 

---

item.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83, above range, setting up Thursday’s Nasdaq debut as ANT
item.description:
How ANT trades on debut is likely to shape sentiment across the wider AI complex. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Amazon and Google are all investors, partners or suppliers, so their shares may react to how ANT opens. Asian chip and memory stocks that supply AI hardware could feel the knock-on effect in Friday’s session. Rates are the main risk to the AI trade. With several Fed officials leaning toward further hikes, any rise in Treasury yields would sharpen worries about funding costs for data centres and neoclouds. A strong debut could ease those worries for now, while a soft one would add to them.

---

Anthropic’s above-range pricing shows the big money is keen, but Thursday’s opening trade will show whether public markets agree, at a time when AI stocks are already uneasy about rates, politics and leadership upheaval.

Summary:

  • Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the $70 to $78 range it set last week
  • Trading is expected to begin on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19, with no scheduled time for the first trade (in case you are wondering)
  • Amazon and Google each hold stakes worth more than $100 billion, and a big tech group agreed to invest $26 billion in the offering
  • Revenue for the nine months to September was around $33 billion, up roughly 1,200%, and run-rate revenue reached about $81 billion in October
  • The nine-month net loss was around $104 billion, mostly from fair-value changes on convertible notes and derivatives
  • The listing comes after recent shocks to the AI sector, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and worries that rising rates will raise funding costs

Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, above the $70 to $78 range it set last week, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The Claude developer is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19.

There is no scheduled time for the first trade. That is normal for an IPO: a new listing opens only once the exchange and the underwriters have matched enough buy and sell orders to set an opening price, which can take anywhere from minutes to several hours after the regular session begins.

Pricing above the range points to strong institutional demand, and it comes at a sensitive moment for the artificial intelligence trade. The sector has been rattled by a run of shocks, including a voter backlash against AI that showed up in the midterm elections and the ouster of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week. Investors were already uneasy that rising interest rates could make debt too expensive for many data centre developers and so-called neoclouds, the specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity.

The deal also ties together much of big tech. Amazon and Google each hold stakes in Anthropic worth more than $100 billion, and a group including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to invest a combined $26 billion in the offering. Anthropic, in turn, is a major buyer of computing systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD, so the reception for ANT shares will be read as a verdict on that whole web of spending.

The growth figures help explain the appetite. Anthropic reported revenue of around $33 billion for the nine months to September 30, up roughly 1,200% from a year earlier, driven largely by demand for its Claude Code programming tool. It said its annualised run-rate revenue reached about $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion in a month. The company booked a net loss of around $104 billion over the nine months, although most of that reflected changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities rather than operating losses.

Investors have plenty to weigh. The prospectus runs to more than 90 pages of risk factors, and the company has had two high-profile disputes with the US government this year over safety, regulation and national security. Competition is also fierce: Anthropic is racing OpenAI and Google for enterprise customers, and OpenAI, which has confidentially filed for its own listing, has said a debut is likely in 2027.

How ANT trades once it opens will show whether public markets share the enthusiasm seen in the book. A strong debut could steady sentiment across AI stocks after a bruising few weeks, while a weak one would feed the doubts about rates, funding costs and stretched valuations that have been building in the sector. 

What is this, a dollar for ANTs?

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kashkari says markets see more Fed hikes than officials do as four Fed voices turn hawkish
item.description:
Hawkish Fed remarks arriving one after another should support the US dollar and keep front-end Treasury yields firm going into December. Gold is the asset most exposed. Through this cycle it has fallen as Fed hike expectations build, so more tightening talk is a headwind rather than a bid. For the Australian dollar, which is already near 10-month lows, a Fed that keeps hiking narrows the policy gap with the RBA. That raises the stakes for today’s Australian jobs data. If Kashkari is right that the shocks behind inflation are supply-driven, oil remains the key input to watch, because further energy price spikes would strengthen the hawks’ case.

---

When a voting Fed official says markets expect more hikes than his colleagues do and makes no effort to push back, the message is that the policy path may have to rise to meet the pricing.

Summary:

  • Minneapolis Fed President Kashkari said markets believe the Fed will need to hike more than officials currently expect
  • He said elevated inflation has come from a series of supply shocks, and that keeping inflation expectations anchored is essential
  • He described the strength of US demand as somewhat surprising and the job market as resilient
  • He said interest rates can clearly affect investment levels
  • Waller, Daly and Barr also sounded hawkish on Wednesday, with Waller again floating a  (not gonna happen, IMHO ;-) ) 50 basis point hike
  • The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, with two dissents in favour of a hike

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari said on Wednesday that markets believe the Fed will have to raise interest rates further than officials currently expect, a notable remark from a policymaker who votes on the Federal Open Market Committee this year. He made no attempt, in the comments reported, to talk that pricing down.

Kashkari traced the current bout of elevated inflation to a series of supply shocks and said the Fed’s priority must be keeping inflation expectations anchored. That framing matters. Central bankers often argue they can look through supply shocks, but only if the public keeps faith that inflation will return to target. When shocks arrive one after another, that faith becomes harder to take for granted, and Kashkari’s emphasis on expectations suggests he sees the risk as real rather than theoretical.

He also said the strength of demand has been a little surprising and described the labour market as resilient. Both points weaken the case for patience. A firm economy gives the Fed room to keep tightening without tipping it into a sharp downturn, and a resilient jobs market removes one of the main arguments a more cautious official might make for pausing. Kashkari added that interest rates can absolutely affect investment, pushing back on any suggestion that higher borrowing costs have lost their bite.

His comments landed on a day when several colleagues were sounding a similar note. Governor Christopher Waller, Governor Michael Barr and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly all struck hawkish tones on Wednesday, with Waller once again raising the possibility of a 50 basis point hike. A move of that size remains an outside possibility rather than the base case, but the fact that it is being discussed openly shows how far the debate has shifted toward the scale of further tightening rather than whether it is needed.

The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% at its late October meeting, with two officials dissenting in favour of a quarter point increase. Since then, hotter inflation data and a steady run of hawkish commentary have reinforced expectations of a hike at the December meeting.

Kashkari’s remark on market pricing is the one to watch. If officials begin publicly endorsing a higher path than their own projections imply, the December forecasts could shift up to meet the market, rather than the market moving back toward the Fed.

There are many more than one of these! A "Fed" of hawks!

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 19, 2026: Australian jobs report preview
item.description:
Greg's preview already:

  • Australia jobs preview. Employment expected to rebound after September’s drop. What technical levels are in play?

My effort follows!

---

---

The Australian dollar goes into the release near 0.6715 (as I post at least), close to its weakest level since January, so the bar for a relief bounce is low. A solid headline gain plus a steady or lower jobless rate would likely bring back some pricing for a February hike and lift the Aussie off its lows. A rise in unemployment to 4.8% or higher would probably extend the slide and pull front-end yields lower as traders price a longer peak. The minutes flagged that oil costs tied to the Middle East conflict could add to inflation, which means a soft print alone may not close the door on further tightening while crude stays elevated.

--- Australia’s jobs report should recover most of September’s part-time losses, but with a divided RBA board split over how close the economy is to a sharper downturn, the unemployment rate matters more than the headline gain.

Summary:

  • Australia’s October employment report is due at 00:30 GMT Thursday (7:30 pm US Eastern Wednesday)
  • Consensus expects about 25,000 jobs added, unemployment steady at 4.7% and participation at 66.8%
  • September’s 39,300 fall came from a 73,700 slump in part-time work, which is widely expected to partly reverse
  • RBA minutes showed a 6-3 vote for November’s hike to 4.85%, with the three dissenters warning of a possible sharper downturn
  • Wages rose 1.1% in the September quarter, the biggest quarterly gain since late 2023, but real wages are still falling
  • Markets have largely priced out a December hike, and February is seen as the next realistic window

Australia’s October labour force report lands at 00:30 GMT on Thursday (7:30 pm US Eastern on Wednesday), and it arrives with more riding on it than a typical monthly print. Economists expect employment to have risen by around 25,000 after September’s surprise 39,300 fall, with the unemployment rate seen steady at 4.7%, a five-year high, and participation unchanged at 66.8%. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics last month showed the decline was driven almost entirely by a 73,700 slump in part-time roles, while full-time jobs actually rose by about 34,000.

That split is the heart of the case for a rebound. CBA expects the part-time drop to reverse, arguing that large swings in part-time work have historically unwound the following month. Its own internal labour data point to October growth of around 18,000, which it describes as a touch below the pace needed to keep unemployment from rising. In other words, even a healthy-looking headline gain could leave the jobless rate drifting higher.

The release follows two days of mixed signals for the Reserve Bank of Australia. Minutes published on Tuesday showed six of nine board members backed November’s 25 basis point hike to 4.85%, the fifth increase of 2026 and the highest cash rate since 2008, judging policy not yet clearly tight enough to contain upside inflation risks. The three dissenters warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn, pointing to the delayed effect of earlier hikes, a bigger-than-expected rise in unemployment and a softening housing market. Wednesday then brought September quarter wages up 1.1%, the largest quarterly gain since late 2023, lifting annual growth to 3.5%, although real wages have now gone backwards for four straight quarters with inflation above 4%.

The data matter because they speak directly to that split. A jobless rate stuck at 4.7%, or lower, would support the majority view that the labour market is loosening only gradually, which Westpac also expects as jobs growth runs below population growth. A rise to 4.8% or beyond would hand the dissenters fresh evidence and make it harder for the hawks to argue for a sixth hike. Several high-profile layoff announcements, including job cuts at NAB, Qantas, Rio Tinto and David Jones, add to the sense of downside risk, though economists note the numbers remain small relative to average monthly hiring.

The RBA’s own forecasts already assume unemployment climbs, reaching 4.9% by the end of this year and a bit above 5% by late 2028, so a modest uptick would not be a shock. The bigger question is the pace. Traders have largely abandoned bets on a December move, and CBA judges the 7 to 8 December meeting will not be live, flagging February as the next realistic window for another hike. A clean rebound in jobs alongside firm wages could keep that February door open, while a second soft month would push the conversation toward how long rates stay at their peak.

Watch the detail as closely as the headline: hours worked, the full-time versus part-time mix and the unrounded jobless rate will all shape how the board reads the print.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market's verdict on Nvidia earnings is a problem for the AI boom trade
item.description:
With each passing day, the probability is rising that the AI boom is coming to an end.

Nvidia reported good earnings yesterday and the guidance was upbeat. At the very least, there was no sign of trouble in the earnings numbers. Shares initially cheered, rising more than 5% after hours but that disappeared at the open and NVDA is now down 2.3% on the day.

The inability to bounce on good news despite a 38% drop in the past month and an undemanding 9x multiple is worrisome.

The price action in Micron and CoreWeave since recent earnings reports makes it look like a pattern.

The optimistic take is that the profits from AI are shifting away from chip and equipment makers to the users, and potentially the labs. Competition is coming for chips and one of the killer apps for AI will surely be designing custom chips and hyper-efficient hardware. So while the profits will likely remain high this year and next, there's a rub pull coming with profits inevitably cratering just as more capacity comes online.

The pessimistic take is that the economics of AI make no sense. Institutional Investor this month laid out the case that AI infrastructure investments could require economic value equivalent to 20% of all global corporate operating profits to justify the spending. And if investment keeps growing at its current assumed pace, the requirement could eventually approach 50%.

That's ludicrous and obvious bubble stuff. It's based on $9 trillion in capex from 2026-2030 and the assumption that every $1 trillion in capex must ultimately create about $1.2 trillion of annual value for customers.

Similarly, a BCG report is particularly interesting because it estimates that current annual AI revenue for the largest hyperscalers is only around $100 billion, versus the $1.6–2 trillion eventually required in its model. That's a 16–20-fold increase.

So the bear case on the whole boom is that people are doing the math and finding it difficult to envision an economic return.

That brings us to the second bullet in this week's AI trade-- the Anthropic IPO. It looks to be pricing well and that should be giving markets a lift but it doesn't seem to be. The bull case is that Anthropic will capture a great deal of the economic value of AI, likely by disrupting incumbents but -- if you believe the IPO hype -- also by curing diseases.

The problem is the starting point. Investors putting a $1.25-$1.75 trillion valuation on it now are already pricing it as one of the most-valuable companies in the world, despite intense competition from open source models, Google, Meta and OpenAI. To score a double, it would need to surpass Amazon in valuation, for a triple it would need to pass Microsoft. There's no path to a 10x in any realistic scenario while the odds of getting wiped out are significant.

That said, it looks like the IPO is going to go well. If that's the case, it needs to be something that calms down the rest of the market because right now it looks like it could be a tipping point towards a rout. 

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: FOMC Minutes: A couple of participants noted a hike of more than 25 bps could warrant consideration in December
item.description:
It sounds like Waller isn't alone in the 50 basis point hike camp.

  • “A couple of participants noted that an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if incoming inflation data were unfavorable.”
  • A few participants who supported no change in rates suggested it was a close call
  • “Some participants” favoured a 25 bp hike at the meeting. Only two members, Cook and Hammack, dissented.
  • “Almost all participants” judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks.
  • A few of those who wanted to hike said they could have accepted a hold as long as markets clearly understood that more tightening was likely.
  • Some participants said market expectations of hikes in December and next year were broadly in line with their own view of the right path.
  • The vast majority saw upside risks to inflation, and many called the AI buildout a “material source of inflation risk.”
  • A majority noted that financial conditions had tightened since the September meeting.
  • Fed staff flagged the risk that inflation expectations could become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation.

The minutes show that the 10-2 vote understated how hawkish this meeting was. In Fed language “some” means more than “a few,” so Cook and Hammack had company among the non-voters. Add the participants who called it a close call and the bloc leaning toward a hike in October was substantial.

This was a conditional hold. Policymakers said outright that market pricing for December was doing part of the work, and several said that alignment was what made it safe to wait. Some of the hawks only accepted a hold because markets were already pricing more hikes.

The most important line is the one about more than 25 bps. A couple of participants said a bigger move could be considered if the inflation data came in unfavorable, and the October CPI did exactly that. Waller set a 0.3% core threshold for 50 bps, and the report met it. These minutes come before that report, so the case for a bigger move has only strengthened since.

The dovish argument rests on financial conditions. Mortgage rates are up, junk spreads have widened sharply, bank shares fell hard, and the market is taking a harder look at AI financing. A couple of officials argued for a gradual approach so households and businesses can adjust. That’s the case for 25 bps in December, but in these minutes it’s the minority view.

The market has 62 bps of hikes priced over the next three meetings, and nothing in these minutes argues against that. If anything, the debate has moved from whether the Fed hikes in December to how much with 27 bps priced in right now and 62 bps at the next three meetings.

His comments come amid an increasingly hawkish debate at the Fed. Policymakers have been grappling with stubborn inflation despite a resilient labor market, raising questions about whether current interest rates are sufficiently restrictive.

item.title: BoC’s Gravelle says policy scenarios help build credibility
item.description:
Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle discussed how the central bank uses scenarios to explain how it might respond as economic conditions change.

  • Bank of Canada scenarios are designed to help keep the BoC accountable and build credibility.
  • When the public trusts the BoC to keep inflation around 2%, their inflation expectations stay anchored.
  • If inflation expectations are anchored, that makes monetary policy more effective.
  • By helping market participants understand how we tend to react when conditions change, we can shape their expectations.
  • Bank of Canada says scenarios help make monetary policy more effective.
  • If businesses expect the BoC will get inflation back down to 2%, they are less likely to build higher inflation into their prices.
  • That decision helps keep inflation in check and reduces barriers to getting it back to target.

Analysis

Gravelle’s point is that credibility can change how businesses set prices today. If they believe the BoC will get inflation back to 2%, they have less reason to raise prices in anticipation of higher costs. That can make an inflation shock less persistent and give monetary policy more traction.

The tone is broadly neutral for the next rate decision. For traders, the focus is on how the BoC might respond if the data change. The scenarios give markets a way to update rate expectations as the outlook evolves.

Hawkish Bias

The tone leans hawkish. The point that stands out is that spending is holding up even at the lower end of the income scale. With consumers still spending and the labor market stable, Daly has room to keep the focus on inflation. For traders, that argues for patience on rate cuts while price pressures remain elevated.

Last week from Daly

Last week, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said the Fed would likely need to raise rates further. Speaking at Stanford on Thursday, Nov. 12, she pointed to inflation spreading into services, where price pressures tend to stick. She also said higher bond yields were already tightening financial conditions, giving the Fed some room to decide when and by how much to move.

That raises the risk that more of those costs get passed on to consumers. Today’s comments fit that hawkish bias. A stable labor market and resilient spending give the Fed room to keep leaning against inflation. item.description:
The USDCAD is pushing to new highs for the day and in the process is trading to a new high going back to April 2025. 

The economic data favors a higher USD

Fundamentally, the recent U.S.–Canada data gap favors a higher USDCAD. U.S. growth and hiring are stronger, while Canada’s latest inflation report showed less pressure underneath the headline. That gives the Fed more reason to tighten than the Bank of Canada.

  • Jobs. U.S. payrolls rose 165K in October versus 65K expected, and unemployment was 4.1%. Canadian employment was essentially flat, and unemployment rose to 6.7% from 6.5%.

  • Growth. U.S. real GDP grew 0.8% quarter over quarter in Q3 (3.4% annualized). Statistics Canada’s preliminary industry-based estimate points to 0.3% quarter-over-quarter growth, with the official Canadian Q3 release due November 30. The Atlanta Fed GDP growth model although lower today at 3.2% from 3.4% is still at 3.2%. 

The market barometer is the two-year yield spread. The U.S. two-year is around 4.8% versus 3.3% in Canada, roughly 150 basis points in favor of the USD. The BoC already raised its policy rate to 2.50% in October, but the softer Canadian CPI weakens the case for a follow-up hike. Meanwhile, Fed Governor Waller is pressing for either a 50 bp hike in December or a clearer signal of faster tightening. The trade talks offer some support for the CAD, but the rate differential gives USDCAD buyers the stronger fundamental argument for now.

U.S.–Canada trade talks are picking up, but there’s still no tariff deal.

President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. They agreed to keep working toward a trade agreement and stay in close contact. Canada’s official readout gave no timeline or details on tariff relief. Prime Minister of Canada

  • The talks are getting more regular. CBC reports that Canadian trade minister Dominic LeBlanc has been speaking weekly with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as officials work through trade disputes.
  • Autos, steel and aluminum are the sectors to watch. Ottawa is seeking relief in those industries. After talks broke down in August, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods, and Canada retaliated.

For USDCAD, I’d read the meeting as modestly CAD-positive. The two sides are talking more regularly, which eases some of the trade uncertainty. A concrete tariff rollback, especially on autos, would be a stronger catalyst for CAD strength and a lower USDCAD. 

Until there is a tariff deal, the market is focusing more on the economic data vs what could be.

USDCAD buyers remain in control

USDCAD has been trending higher since bottoming at 1.3929 on November 4, within shouting distance of its rising 200-day moving average. Pullbacks have been shallow, and buyers have continued to show up at the levels they needed to defend.

The first key break came on November 6, when the price moved above its 100-day moving average ahead of the U.S. and Canadian jobs reports. Stronger U.S. hiring and softer Canadian employment gave the move a fundamental tailwind that saw the price extend above a swing area target between 1.4068 and 1.40801. After moving to a high near 1.4135, the subsequent pullback found buyers in the aforementioned swing area that 1.4068–1.4080, and the trend higher resumed.

Fast forward to this week, and on Monday and Tuesday, the price traded on both sides of another key target at the 1.42918–1.42986 swing area. The market took a breath. However, yesterday’s pullback found willing buyers near the rising 100-hour moving average, setting up a move higher into the close. Today, after extending gains through the Asian and early European sessions, the pair pulled back and found buyers just ahead of 1.4298. That gave buyers another level to lean against, and the price pushed to a new high for the year at 1.4338.

The 61.8% retracement defines close risk

On the daily chart, the move higher has taken the price above 1.42928, the 61.8% retracement of the decline from the February 2025 high to the late-January 2026 low. The pair poked above that level in October and again yesterday, with limited follow-through. Today’s move has carried farther, and 1.42928 now defines close risk for buyers.

Stay above 1.42928, and the bias remains bullish. The next major upside target is the 1.4400 area, where the March and July 2025 swing highs stalled.

What would give the sellers a victory?

A move back below 1.42928 would take some of the upside pressure off and put the focus on the rising 100-hour moving average at 1.42845. A break below that moving average would give sellers a technical victory and put the latest leg higher at risk. As long as the price holds above both levels, buyers remain in control.

Trading lesson. The break gets your attention. The pullback tells you more.

USDCAD traded above the 61.8% retracement at 1.42928 back in October, but the buyers could not build momentum. This time, the price broke higher, pulled back toward the old swing area and found willing buyers. It then extended to a new high for the year at 1.4338. Seeing buyers defend former resistance on a pullback gives traders more confidence in the break.

The pullback also gives traders a level to lean against. In this case, 1.42928 defines close risk. A move back below it would put traders on alert. A break below the rising 100-hour moving average at 1.42845 would give the sellers a clearer technical victory.

That’s how I put together the bias, the risk and the target. Above 1.42928, the bias stays higher and 1.4400 is the next major target. Below the 100-hour moving average, I’d reassess the bullish bias even if the broader uptrend is still intact.

item.description:

Private oil inventory data released late yesterday showed:

  • Crude +5300K
  • Gasoline +5100K
  • Distillates +400K

WTI crude oil was down $1.25 to $84.76 ahead of the report and extended losses by 50-cents afterwards.

For background, the US Energy Information Administration releases its Weekly Petroleum Status Report every Wednesday at 10:30 am ET, or Thursday in holiday-shortened weeks. Covering the week that ended the prior Friday, it’s the most closely watched regular data point for the oil market and one of the few energy reports that reliably moves crude prices.

The headline number is the weekly change in US commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Markets measure it against analyst estimates, with bigger-than-expected builds generally weighing on prices and surprise draws supporting them. Inventories at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for the WTI futures contract, get separate scrutiny because tight stocks there can squeeze the front of the futures curve.

The report goes well beyond crude. It tracks gasoline and distillate stockpiles, refinery throughput and utilization rates, domestic crude production, and imports and exports. Product supplied, a proxy for demand, shows how much gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products are moving into the market. Changes in the SPR are listed separately, since they reflect government purchases or releases rather than commercial supply and demand.

Weekly swings can be large and misleading. A delayed tanker or a shift in export timing can produce a multimillion-barrel build or draw that reverses the next week, and production figures are estimates rather than direct counts. Traders tend to weigh the combined change in crude and products, compare stocks with seasonal norms and focus on multi-week trends.

The American Petroleum Institute’s private survey, released Tuesdays at 4:30 pm ET, offers an early preview. The two reports often disagree, but the EIA figures are the official benchmark and usually set the tone for crude trading.

item.description:

That 16.7% number is awful and highlights how the pricing in the market is hanging by a thread. It won't get any easier in the months ahead if the Fed keeps hiking either. Today Waller renewed his call for 50 basis points.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun.

“Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

For background, the National Association of Realtors publishes its Pending Home Sales Index monthly at 10 am ET, usually near the end of the month. It tracks signed contracts to buy existing homes, including single-family homes, condos and co-ops, making it the most forward-looking piece of NAR’s monthly housing data.

The index is benchmarked so that 100 equals the average level of contract activity in 2001, a year NAR considers a normal, balanced market. Readings are seasonally adjusted and reported as monthly and year-over-year changes. Results are also broken down by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West.

Because a home sale typically closes one to two months after a contract is signed, pending sales lead NAR’s existing home sales report, which counts completed closings. Economists use the index to gauge where existing home sales are headed. The relationship isn’t perfect. Some contracts fall through because of financing problems, failed inspections or appraisal gaps, and cancellation rates can rise when mortgage rates jump or buyers get cold feet.

Contract signings are highly sensitive to mortgage rates, so the index often responds quickly to moves in Treasury yields. A drop in rates can show up in pending sales within weeks, well before it appears in closings or prices.

The report rarely moves broader markets, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder and mortgage-related stocks and as an early read on housing demand. In recent years, the index has hovered near historically low levels as high mortgage rates, stretched affordability and the lock-in effect, where homeowners are reluctant to give up low-rate mortgages, have kept buyers and sellers on the sidelines.

item.title: Macro signals from today's earnings: Target, TJX and Lowe’s
item.description:
Eyes are on the US consumer this week and yesterday's Home Depot numbers and government retail sales data were solid. Today it's more of the same with Target, TJX and Lowe’s reports pointing the same way. Spending is holding up better than expected. For this trio, it was coming from more shoppers rather than higher prices while big-ticket spending tied to housing is still weak.

Target (the strongest macro read):

  • This was Target’s best sales growth in five years. Comps rose 5.6% against 3.8% expected, driven by a 5% jump in traffic, while the average ticket rose just 0.6%. That’s an excellent signal on a broadening of volume, and not price hikes.
  • CEO Fiddelke said "It’s not just one consumer... The broad-based nature — by geography, by guest demographic, by income level — gives us confidence”. 
  • Target cited U.S. shoppers’ worries about the economy and their own finances as a reason it promoted price cuts this year, and cut prices on nearly 2,000 more items in the third quarter and is promoting sub $20 Christmas gifts. Apparel and home are still weak, and a year ago comps were -2.7%, so the comp was easy.

TJX (Canada strong)

  • Comparable sales rose 4% against a 2–3% guide. Somewhat worrisome was that the US was +2%, versus +6% a year earlier. HomeGoods was +5%, Canada +6% and International +8%
  • Q4 comps are guided to +2–3%. The full-year comp was raised to 4% from 3% to 4%.
  • Strip out tariff refunds and gross margin fell 0.5 pts on freight and fuel. Adjusted pretax margin slipped 0.2 pts to 12.5%.
  • Management called merchandise availability “outstanding.” That’s code for other retailers sitting on excess goods, which is disinflationary for apparel and home.

Lowe’s (housing still stuck)

  • Comparable sales rose 1.8%, above the 0.4% consensus, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and solid sales to professional customers and home services
  • The full-year comp moved up to about +0.5% from flat, but operating margin guidance slipped to about 11.1% from 11.2%.
  • CEO Ellison told CNBC Lowe’s “can grow” despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He had previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year
  • Gross margin fell 124 bps to 32.95% even with ~$250m in tariff refunds. That implies an underlying hit of more than 2 pts

At last check, here were the pre-market changes in the trio: 

  • TGT +0.3%
  • TJX +5.9%
  • LOW -5.6%

You can see the market had built in beats on comp sales, which is part of the usual sandbagging. From a purely macro perspective though, the signals were solid, particularly from Target. There is no sign the consumer is meaningfully weakening, though Christmas is the big test.

We get Walmart earnings tomorrow and that's the strongest macro view you will get from a retailer. S&P 500 futures are up 0.35% but that's all about Nvidia.

item.title: US October housing starts 1.309M vs 1.245M expected
item.description:
• Prior was 1.221M
  • Starts change +9.9% vs -5.2% prior
  • Building permits 1.295M vs 1.377M expected
  • Prior permits 1.398M
  • Permits change -7.4% m/m vs vs -0.4% prior

This is a rare win in US housing data and runs counter to rising mortgage rates and a long string of poor reports, including rock-bottom homebuilder sentiment. I would take it as a one-off until further notice, particularly with the fall in forward-looking permits.

For background, the US Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development publish the New Residential Construction report monthly at 8:30 am ET, usually in the third week of the month. It’s released the day after the NAHB homebuilder sentiment index and offers the first hard data on new home construction each month.

The headline figure is housing starts, the number of new privately owned homes on which construction began, reported as a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. The report also includes building permits, which are issued before construction begins and are generally viewed as a better leading indicator of future activity. It also covers completions, homes authorized but not yet started, and units under construction.

Starts and permits are split between single-family homes and buildings with five or more units. The multifamily category is highly volatile because a handful of large apartment projects can swing the monthly figure, so markets tend to focus on single-family starts and permits for the underlying trend. Results are also broken down by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West.

The monthly data have wide margins of error, and changes in a single month are frequently not statistically significant. Revisions can be large, which is why economists tend to look at three-month averages.

Housing starts feed into residential investment, a component of GDP that’s highly sensitive to interest rates and often leads the broader business cycle. The report rarely moves markets dramatically, but it shapes the outlook for homebuilders and suppliers. Mortgage rates, affordability, construction costs, tariffs on building materials and labor availability are the main forces driving the data.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Waller calls for more aggressive action to break psychology that 3% inflation is the norm
item.description:
Fed Governor Waller is becoming increasingly concerned about the US inflation outlook, warning that price pressures are broadening beyond energy and that the Fed risks allowing higher inflation to become entrenched in consumers' and businesses' expectations.

Waller argues that the central bank needs to take a more aggressive action to convince markets and the public that it remains committed to bringing inflation back to its 2% target.

He highlighted that roughly 70% of components in the core services basket are currently experiencing inflation above 3%, suggesting that price pressures are no longer concentrated in energy-related categories.

He is concerned that businesses are becoming comfortable passing higher prices on to consumers, partly because they believe consumers remain resilient enough to absorb those increases.

If businesses expect to raise prices and consumers increasingly accept 3% inflation as normal, inflation expectations could become more entrenched, making it harder for the Fed to bring inflation back down, without a more aggressive tightening.

He thinks the Fed needs to break the psychology that inflation around 3% has become the new norm after failing to bring it back to the 2% target since 2021. He stressed that the Fed needs to become more aggressive, either by delivering a 50 bps rate hike or use monetary policy communications to signal a significantly tougher stance in the months ahead.

Simply maintaining the current policy trajectory might not be enough to change inflation expectations. The Fed needs to convince businesses, consumers and financial markets that it is prepared to take stronger action to restore price stability. He even suggested that the central bank might need to go beyond reversing the rate cuts implemented last year to bring inflation under control.

He also argued that the Fed should use statements, press conferences and forward guidance to steer market expectations towards a more restrictive policy outlook. A hawkish communication strategy could push interest rate expectations higher and tightening financial conditions enough to weigh on economic activity and inflation.

He also questioned the usefulness of the December Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), arguing that year-end projections might not adequately capture the evolving inflation picture. He prefers adopting a more forceful and forward-looking communication strategy rather than relying too heavily on projections that could quickly become outdated.

For now, Waller remains the only governor suggesting a more aggressive action, with the majority of Fed members preferring to move in small steps. Nevertheless, he's been a very influential member and his views have always preceded a change in monetary policy since 2021. 

In the current context, traders should be very careful buying risk assets unless the Iran war ends or the Fed turns surprisingly dovish. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
